name: zpoline (x86-64 system call hook by binary rewriting)
baseline: ptrace-based system call interception (README headline); Intel Pin System Call API (reviewer Q&A in Documentation/README.md)
workload: Per-system-call hook overhead on Linux x86-64 with an empty hook function, measured with the getpid benchmark of Section 3.2 of the USENIX ATC 2023 paper (the benchmark program is not in the repository; apps/basic only prints syscall numbers).
claimed_speedup: README: '100 times faster than ptrace.' Documentation/README.md: zpoline hook overhead 41 ns (paper Table 1) against 2629 ns for the Intel Pin System Call API (2703 ns per getpid minus 74 ns for the kernel getpid), about 64x (derived from page data); a later trampoline change (0xeb 0x6a 0x90 instead of nops, May 2023) gives 10 ns, '4 times faster than the previous version'; the reviewer-suggested short-jump variant gave 31 ns.
tradeoffs: Linux on x86-64 only. Replaces the two-byte syscall/sysenter instructions in loaded code with callq *%rax and plants a nop-sled trampoline at virtual address 0, so /proc/sys/vm/mmap_min_addr must be set to 0 (the README also reports mmap failures under SELinux). Uses the libopcodes disassembler from binutils to find the instructions. Rewritten code pages can no longer be shared between processes (glibc-2.35 has 544 syscall/sysenter instructions across 62 pages). Hook functions must avoid issuing rewritten syscalls or they loop forever. NULL-pointer writes no longer fault by default (mitigations exist).
caveats: Category fit is weak: this is syscall-interception tooling built on instruction rewriting, not an assembler or disassembler, and the baselines (ptrace, Intel Pin) are not GNU as, NASM or MASM. The 100x headline has no table, hardware, kernel version or compiler flags on the README page. The 41 ns, 2629 ns and 10 ns figures come from the repo's Documentation page and quote the paper's Table 1 (paper not opened: usenix.org is not reachable here); the CPU is only called 'our hardware'. The 64x ratio mixes the paper's zpoline run with a Pin run done later for the reviews, so the two were possibly measured on different days. The getpid benchmark program is not in the repository. The last commit is from January 2025.

name: svc-hook (ARM64 system call hook by binary rewriting)
baseline: ptrace-based system call interception on ARM64
workload: System call interception on ARM64 Linux, Android, FreeBSD and NetBSD by rewriting every svc instruction in the loaded target to a b instruction that branches to a per-instruction trampoline; the README compares hook cost with ptrace.
claimed_speedup: README Key Features: '1,000 times faster than `ptrace`'. No ptrace timing appears on the page. Documentation/README.md reports only the cost of hooking against unhooked runs: SQLite per-operation time up 0.01% to 2.6%, PostgreSQL pgbench 10790 TPS hooked against 10923 TPS unhooked (1.2% reduction), Samba file transfer throughput down 0.9% (download) and 0.1% (upload).
hardware: Documentation experiments: HoneyComb LX2 board, NXP LX2160A 16-core Arm Cortex-A72 up to 2.2 GHz, 64 GB DRAM, Linux 5.10 (the ptrace claim itself states no hardware).
tradeoffs: ARM64 only (Linux, Android, FreeBSD, NetBSD). Needs no kernel support but rewrites code in memory: svc to b has a +-128 MiB branch range, so one trampoline of 28 bytes per svc instruction is instantiated (20812 bytes for 728 svc instructions in the test setup). FreeBSD and NetBSD need procfs mounted at /proc and NetBSD needs PaX mprotect restrictions disabled.
caveats: Category fit is weak: syscall-interception tooling built on instruction rewriting, not an assembler or disassembler, and ptrace is not GNU as, NASM or MASM. The 1,000x figure is one README bullet with no method, hardware, kernel or command; the supplementary Documentation page measures overhead against unhooked runs, not against ptrace. The associated paper (Middleware 2025) was not opened (dl.acm.org is not reachable here). Language is inferred from main.c and the Makefile because the repo page shows no language bar.
